entities.name: Safavid Empire
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Safavid Empire (1501–1736) was a Persian imperial dynasty that established Twelver Shia Islam as the state religion of Iran — a decision that permanently defined Iranian national identity and created the Sunni-Shia divide shaping the Middle East today. Founded by Ismail I, who conquered much of Persia by age 14, the Safavids made Iran Shia when 90% of its population was Sunni.

Shah Ismail I's conversion of Iran to Shia Islam, accomplished through military conquest, religious coercion, and systematic killing of Sunni religious scholars, was one of history's most consequential acts of religious policy. The Safavid-Ottoman wars, motivated partly by Sunni-Shia rivalry, defined the Middle Eastern political landscape for two centuries. Shah Abbas I (r.1587-1629) made Isfahan his capital, creating one of the world's most beautiful cities, and built the Safavid empire to its greatest territorial extent.

The Safavid Empire fostered Persian art, literature, and architecture at extraordinary levels: Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Shah Mosque (1611-1629), and Ali Qapu Palace represent the apex of Safavid aesthetics. Persian became the literary language of Mughal India and Ottoman courts. The empire's decline under later weak rulers and the 1722 Afghan Ghilzai invasion ended Safavid rule, though Iran's Shia identity — their most enduring creation — defines Iranian civilization.
